It addresses four research questions: (1) What conserved and species-specific miRNA-mediated mechanisms govern rabies disease? (2) What contextual factors determine antiviral vs. proviral roles of miRNAs in rabies? (3) To what extent do circulating miRNA signatures offer diagnostic and prognostic utility for rabies? (4) What translational barriers prevent clinical implementation of miRNA-based strategies for rabies, and how can the One Health framework help overcome them?
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review integrates three interconnected dimensions: molecular mechanisms, pathogen-specific responses, and translational applications. It synthesizes evidence across rabies virus, rabies infection, and related entities such as PRRSV, avian oncogenic viruses (MDV, ALV), immunosuppressive IBDV, FMD, BVDV, Ebola, Hendra, Rabies, and aquatic viral diseases. The review does not explicitly report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but presents a critical narrative synthesis.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Key findings include: (a) a four-axis contextual framework (cell type, infection stage, viral strain, host-viral miRNA competition) that explains the antiviral/proviral duality of miRNAs in rabies; (b) virus-encoded miRNAs (v-miRNAs) as lower-risk therapeutic targets due to their absence from uninfected host genomes; (c) circulating miRNA biomarkers validated only at proof-of-concept stage (TRL 1-3), with no veterinary product yet at TRL ≥4; and (d) zoonotic conservation of miR-155, miR-146a, miR-21, and miR-122 across human and veterinary pathogens, supporting a 'One miRNA, One Health' convergence strategy.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that while miRNA research has advanced, a comprehensive and critically integrated understanding of their biological functions and clinical applications across veterinary viral diseases, including rabies, remains incomplete. Additionally, the review notes that circulating miRNA signatures have only been validated at proof-of-concept stage, with no veterinary product yet at TRL ≥4, indicating a gap in clinical implementation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Critical short-term priorities include standardized pre-analytical protocols, open-access veterinary miRNA databases, and multicenter validation in natural infection cohorts. These efforts aim to improve the reliability and applicability of miRNA-based diagnostics and therapeutics for rabies.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in rabies virus and rabies disease, focusing on molecular mechanisms, pathogen-specific responses, and translational applications. It presents a four-axis contextual framework to explain the antiviral/proviral duality of miRNAs and highlights the potential of virus-encoded miRNAs as therapeutic targets. The review also identifies the need for standardized protocols, open-access databases, and multicenter validation to advance miRNA-based diagnostics and therapeutics for rabies. Despite progress, the review notes that circulating miRNA signatures have only reached proof-of-concept stage, and no veterinary product has achieved TRL ≥4. The 'One miRNA, One Health' convergence strategy is proposed to leverage the zoonotic conservation of specific miRNAs across human and veterinary pathogens.

title: Antigenic landscape of rabies and related lyssaviruses revealed by cryo-EM.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies continues to kill over 60,000 people per year despite life-saving vaccines and post-exposure treatments and costs billions of dollars in prevention and treatment.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: We find that these antigenic sites, V and VI, are broadly cross-reactive across lyssaviruses, whereas immunodominant sites II/IV and III are rabies specific.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Together, these results provide a roadmap for structure-guided vaccine and therapeutic antibody design for rabies and related lyssaviruses.

title: Safety, Immunogenicity, Antibody Persistence, and Booster Responses of an Animal-Component-Free Vero Cell Rabies Vaccine: A Randomized, Active-Controlled Phase III Trial.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the safety and immunogenicity of an animal-component-free, antibiotic-free, freeze-dried human rabies vaccine (Vero Cell) with the "Essen" regimen and boosted two doses in China. Abstract Background Eliminating animal-source additives from vaccine manufacture may reduce dependence on variable biological raw materials and the theoretical risk of adventitious-agent or extraneous-protein contamination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: 1,200 healthy participants aged 10–60 years were randomized into two groups to receive the test vaccine or a licensed freeze-dried human Rabies Vaccine (Vero Cell) with the five doses Essen regimen. Additionally, samples were obtained before (months 3 or 12 respectively) and after two doses booster regimen.
analysis.methods: Rabies virus-neutralizing antibody (RVNA) concentrations were measured by the rapid fluorescent focus inhibition test (RFFIT). Blood samples for immunogenicity assessment were collected pre-vaccination, on day 7 and 14 following the first dose, and day 14 and months 3, 6, and 12 following the final dose of the primary regimen.
analysis.main_results: Out of 1,200 randomized participants, 596 in the test group and 600 in the control group included in the final safety analysis (SS). The test vaccine induced a significantly higher early seroconversion rate and geometric mean concentration (GMC) at Day 7 post-first dose. By Day 14 post-first dose and post-primary series, both groups achieved 100% seroconversion and comparable peak GMCs, with non-inferiority of the two groups. Over the 12-month persistence period, seroconversion rates remained high to 98% in both groups, with GMCs declining in parallel.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The animal-component-free test human rabies vaccine (Vero Cell) induced non-inferior immunogenicity to the licensed vaccine following the primary Essen regimen, maintained RVNA responses at least one year, and elicited robust responses to two-dose boosting even after a prolonged interval to 12 months. These pivotal data establish the clinical performance of a manufacturing platform that avoids animal-source additives.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings demonstrate that the animal-component-free vaccine is a viable alternative to the licensed vaccine, with comparable immunogenicity and safety, which can inform the development of rabies vaccines that reduce reliance on animal-source materials and enhance manufacturing consistency.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: We acknowledge that retrospective registration deviates from the ICMJE requirement for prospective registration and consider this a limitation of our study. The evidence is strong, with a large sample size and clear non-inferiority results, but the retrospective registration may affect the perceived rigor of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of an animal-component-free Vero Cell rabies vaccine compared to a licensed vaccine in a Phase III trial involving 1,200 participants in China. The vaccine was administered using the Essen regimen with two booster doses at 3 and 12 months. Results showed that the test vaccine achieved a significantly higher early seroconversion rate and geometric mean concentration (GMC) at Day 7 post-first dose, but both groups had 100% seroconversion and comparable GMCs by Day 14 post-primary series. Over 12 months, seroconversion rates remained high (98%) in both groups, with parallel GMC declines. Safety assessments found that adverse reactions were primarily mild, and no serious adverse events were reported. The study concluded that the animal-component-free vaccine is non-inferior to the licensed vaccine, maintains robust antibody responses for at least one year, and shows strong boosting effects even after a 12-month interval. The retrospective registration of the trial was noted as a limitation, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and clear non-inferiority results.

title: RABV P protein activates the GSK3β-NF-κB signaling pathway to promote viral replication by interacting with the host protein Snapin.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies virus (RABV), a lethal neurotropic pathogen, relies on interaction with the host to sustain neuronal infection; however, how it balances replication with neuronal survival remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated the role of Snapin, a neuronal trafficking regulator, in RABV replication using N2a cells and infected mice.
analysis.methods: The researchers examined RABV infection effects on Snapin expression and used mechanistic studies to identify interactions between RABV P protein and Snapin, as well as the recruitment of GSK3β and activation of the NF-κB pathway.
analysis.main_results: RABV infection upregulated Snapin expression in N2a cells, and Snapin promoted the replication of RABV CVS11 and SRV9 strains in a dose-dependent manner. The P protein interacts with the 37–78 aa domain of Snapin via its C-terminal domain (172–297 aa), recruits GSK3β in a Snapin-dependent manner, and forms a tripartite complex. Upon complex formation, the phosphorylation level at the Tyr216 site of GSK3β is increased, leading to activation of the NF-κB pathway. Such activation upregulates neuronal stability genes (Septin2, B4gat1, and Disc1), thereby promoting viral replication without eliciting interferon responses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study reveals that RABV exploits Snapin as a molecular scaffold linking P to GSK3β/NF-κB signaling, coupling viral replication to neuronal homeostasis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study identifies a host-dependent axis for therapeutic targeting in rabies treatment and offers broader implications for understanding neurotropic pathogens utilizing analogous mechanisms.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study provides strong evidence from both in vitro and in vivo experiments, but the generalizability of findings to other viral strains or host species remains to be determined.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how rabies virus (RABV) balances replication with neuronal survival by exploiting the host protein Snapin. The research reveals that RABV infection upregulates Snapin expression in N2a cells, and Snapin promotes viral replication in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistic studies show that the RABV P protein interacts with Snapin, recruits GSK3β, and forms a tripartite complex that activates the NF-κB pathway, enhancing viral replication without triggering interferon responses. In vivo experiments demonstrate that reducing Snapin levels in infected mice delays symptom onset and improves survival. These findings highlight a novel Snapin-dependent GSK3β/NF-κB axis as a potential therapeutic target for rabies treatment, offering insights into how neurotropic pathogens manipulate host pathways for their benefit. However, the study's results may not be universally applicable to other viral strains or host species.

title: Mismatched and underrepresented: bat–virus diversity and phylogeographic bias in experimental infection studies

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on rabies virus and rabies disease. It examines the biases in experimental infection studies (EIS) regarding the taxonomic and geographic representation of bat species and viruses, particularly in relation to rabies virus. The central question is whether current EIS adequately reflect the diversity and phylogeography of bat–virus interactions relevant to rabies virus.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review conducted a systematic literature search from January 1900 to January 2025, manually curating peer-reviewed primary studies of viral experimental infections in live bats and bat-derived cell lines (BdCL). From 545 candidate records, 127 papers were retained, comprising 315 unique bat–virus trials. The authors categorized host taxonomy, viral family (ICTV), and biogeographical congruence to quantify temporal trends, taxonomic coverage, and host–virus pairing patterns.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The results show that rabies virus and related entities are underrepresented in EIS, with only 45 of ~1,500 bat species (3.2%) and 7 of 21 bat families appearing in these studies. Pteropodidae, Vespertilionidae, Phyllostomidae, and Molossidae dominate studies, with Rousettus aegyptiacus, Tadarida brasiliensis, and Eptesicus fuscus most frequently trialed. Viral focus is uneven, with Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae (notably rabies [RABV] and influenza A [IAV]) accounting for many trials, and filoviruses being overrepresented in Rousettus sp.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights geographic biases, with high representation in Arctic–Siberian, Eurasian, and North American regions, while Amazonian, Indo-Malayan, Australasian, Papua–Melanesian, and Madagascan regions are poorly represented. These biases limit the inference about host competence, immune diversity, and coevolutionary dynamics, as well as overgeneralize results across Chiroptera. The authors also note that experimental pairings often do not reflect co-evolved host–virus relationships, which constrains mechanistic inference relevant to zoonotic emergence and conservation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: To improve ecological relevance and generalizability, the authors recommend expanding taxonomic and geographic sampling, situating more work within the native ranges of viruses, and integrating complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches. They also emphasize the need for investments in regional biosafety infrastructure and standardized protocols to address these critical gaps.

analysis.summary_en: This review highlights the biases in experimental infection studies (EIS) regarding rabies virus and related entities. It shows that only a small fraction of bat species and families are represented in EIS, with a focus on certain taxa and geographic regions. The review identifies the overrepresentation of Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae, particularly rabies [RABV], and notes the underrepresentation of other regions and species. These biases limit the inference about host competence, immune tolerance, and zoonotic risk. The authors recommend expanding sampling to include more diverse bat species and geographic regions, integrating complementary methods, and investing in biosafety infrastructure and standardized protocols to improve the ecological and evolutionary understanding of rabies virus and its interactions with bats.

title: An applicable and efficient retrograde monosynaptic circuit mapping tool for larval zebrafish.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an efficient method for tracing neural circuits in larval zebrafish, addressing the challenge of monitoring and manipulating whole-brain neuronal activity in this model.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on larval zebrafish, utilizing an applicable methodology tailored for this species to achieve efficient retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracing from genetically defined neurons.
analysis.methods: The methodology involved combinatorial optimization of multiple factors to identify the optimal combination of CVS strain trans-complemented with advanced expression of N2cG at 36 °C for efficient retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracing.
analysis.main_results: The study identified the CVS strain trans-complemented with advanced expression of N2cG at 36 °C as the optimal combination, achieving a tracing efficiency of up to 20 inputs per starter cell.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a novel methodology for efficient retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracing in larval zebrafish, a vertebrate model for in vivo monitoring of neuronal activity. The approach involves combinatorial optimization to identify the optimal combination of a CVS strain trans-complemented with advanced expression of N2cG at 36 °C, achieving a tracing efficiency of up to 20 inputs per starter cell. The method enables cell-type-specific input tracing and circuit reconstruction, with low cytotoxicity allowing for viable labeling and calcium imaging of infected neurons up to 10 days post-infection. The findings highlight the potential of this technique for studying neural circuits in larval zebrafish, which could inform broader research on brain function and disease. However, the study is based on abstract-only data, and its applicability to other systems remains to be determined, limiting the evidence strength to moderate.

title: Profil Epidemiologi Kasus Gigitan Hewan Penular Rabies (GHPR) di Wilayah Kerja Puskesmas Kauditan, Kabupaten Minahasa Utara, Sulawesi Utara

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rabies is a contagious disease caused by a virus. If rabies cases are not promptly managed, they can result in death. The study aimed to identify and describe the epidemiological profile of Rabies-Transmitting Animal Bites (RTAB) in the working area of Kauditan Health Center, North Minahasa Regency, North Sulawesi Province.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This research employed a descriptive observational design with a cross-sectional approach. The sample consisted of 63 patients with GHPR recorded at Kauditan Health Center during the period of January to June 2025. Total sampling was used, meaning the entire population was included as the sample.
analysis.methods: After approval, secondary data were collected from medical records. The data obtained were presented in tabular form accompanied by explanations and organized according to the research objectives.
analysis.main_results: From January to June 2025, Kauditan Health Center reported 63 cases of Rabies-Transmitting Animal Bites (RTAB), with the majority occurring in males (36 cases, 57.14%) compared to females (27 cases, 42.86%). The most affected age group was children aged 1–10 years, accounting for 24 cases (38.1%). Dogs were identified as the primary transmitters, responsible for 53 cases (84.13%), while cats accounted for 10 cases (15.87%). The most frequent bite locations were the fingers (30.2%) and hands (28.6%), indicating that bites predominantly occurred on the upper limbs within the Kauditan Health Center’s jurisdiction.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that males were more frequently affected by RTAB than females, and children aged 1–10 years were the most affected age group. Dogs were the primary transmitters, with fingers and hands being the most common bite locations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and prevention strategies for RTAB in the Kauditan Health Center’s jurisdiction. Understanding the epidemiological profile of RTAB can help in developing targeted interventions to reduce the incidence of rabies in the community.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s design limitations include the use of secondary data, which may introduce bias. The sample size was relatively small, and the findings may not be generalizable to other areas. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study identified and described the epidemiological profile of Rabies-Transmitting Animal Bites (RTAB) in Kauditan Health Center, North Minahasa Regency, North Sulawesi Province. It found that males were more frequently affected, with children aged 1–10 years being the most affected age group. Dogs were the primary transmitters, and fingers and hands were the most common bite locations. The findings can inform surveillance and prevention strategies for RTAB.

title: Health-facility readiness and provider-perceived barriers and facilitators to animal-bite management in Mangalore, India: a mixed-methods study

analysis.scope_and_question: Rabies virus and rabies disease. The study focuses on health-facility readiness and provider-perceived barriers and facilitators to animal-bite management in Mangalore, India. The central question is how facility readiness and provider perspectives affect the delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A convergent mixed-methods study was conducted in six urban primary health centres (PHCs) and one district-hospital animal-bite clinic. Facility readiness was assessed using a checklist adapted from NAPRE 2030 and IPHS 2022. Nine providers (five medical officers and four staff nurses) were interviewed purposively. Quantitative and qualitative data were analysed separately and integrated through a joint display and narrative triangulation.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In the sampled urban facilities, point-in-time vaccine and cold-chain readiness coexisted with important gaps in HRIG access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, documentation and continuity of supply. Facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are required to improve delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Evidence exploring healthcare provider’s perspectives alongside facility preparedness remains limited. Stock-register review showed at least one ARV stock-out during the preceding six months in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%); the district hospital reported none. HRIG and a designated wound-washing station were unavailable in all 6/6 PHCs (0%) but available at the district-hospital clinic. Nursing staffing met the applicable norm in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%) and at the district hospital.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, competing staff responsibilities, wage-related non-adherence and local adaptive practices were identified as key issues affecting provider adherence to rabies post-exposure protocols.

analysis.summary_en: This mixed-methods study examines health-facility readiness and provider-perceived barriers to animal-bite management in Mangalore, India, focusing on rabies virus and rabies disease. The study highlights that while anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) is physically available in all sampled facilities, there are gaps in human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, and continuity of supply. Provider interviews reveal challenges such as referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, and wage-related non-adherence. The findings suggest that facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are essential to improve the delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care. The study underscores the need for targeted research and practice improvements to address these gaps in rabies management.
